```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

AI coding assistants write R code quickly, but they do not know how a WildObs data package
is built. Left to guess, an assistant may count every row of `observations` as a detection
(blanks and people included), join tables on the wrong key, or treat a 100-day deployment
as a whole survey. WildObsR ships a *skill* for [Claude](https://claude.ai): a short,
plain-text guide to the data that Claude reads before it writes code for you. This
vignette shows what the skill contains, how to install it, and how to check it yourself.

## What the skill covers

The skill describes the data a public API key downloads, and nothing else. It covers:

- how the `deployments`, `observations`, `media` and `covariates` tables join, and on
  which keys;
- what each field means, including the fields WildObs adds to Camtrap DP, such as
  `deploymentGroups`, `multiSeason_deploymentGroup` and the covariates measured at five
  buffer scales;
- which observations to filter out before counting detections, and why obscured
  threatened-species records cannot be placed on a camera;
- what the data can and cannot support: for example, occupancy and abundance models,
  but not spatial capture-recapture, because individual identities, sex and age are
  almost never recorded.

The skill is documentation only. It contains no code and no data, and it never sees your
API key.

## Read it first

The skill ships inside WildObsR, so you can read every file before installing it:

```{r files}
# view where the skill sits in your installed copy of WildObsR
skill_dir <- system.file("claude-skills", "wildobsr-data", package = "WildObsR")

# view its files: an overview, and field-by-field reference tables
list.files(skill_dir, recursive = TRUE)
```

```{r head}
# view the first lines of the overview, which tell Claude when to use the skill
cat(head(readLines(file.path(skill_dir, "SKILL.md")), 14), sep = "\n")
```

## Install it

`install_claude_skill()` copies the skill into `~/.claude/skills`, where
[Claude Code](https://docs.claude.com/en/docs/claude-code) finds it in every project.
Start a new Claude Code session afterwards to use it.

```{r install, eval = FALSE}
WildObsR::install_claude_skill()
```

After you update WildObsR, install the matching version of the skill:

```{r update, eval = FALSE}
WildObsR::install_claude_skill(overwrite = TRUE)
```

To keep the skill within a single project instead, point `dest` at that project's
`.claude/skills` folder, for example
`install_claude_skill(dest = ".claude/skills")`.

## Use it well

Claude uses the skill when a request mentions WildObs data, data packages or their
fields. It still helps to say what you are doing, for example *"I downloaded three WildObs
projects with wildobs_dp_download(); count independent detections of feral cats per
camera"*. Treat the code it writes as you would a colleague's: run it on the bundled
`example_datapackages()` first, and check the counts against what you expect.

The skill's numbers (how many projects, how complete each field is) describe the public
database when that version of WildObsR was built, and drift as the database grows. The
database itself is always the authority.
